Diffraction tomography (DT) is more sensitive than scattering cross-section (SCS) for detecting invisibility cloaks.
DT uses multiple illumination angles and processes both phase and amplitude of scattered waves.
The study analyzed three types of cloaks: scattering cancellation (SC), blow-up-a-point transformation optics (TO), and polygonal TO cloaks.
The diffraction limit for DT in this study is λ/√2 when only forward scattering is measured.
250 projections were used for DT imaging, with at least 8 points per λ sampled for each projection.
The maximum contrast between object and background RI was fixed at 5% for simulations.
For SC cloaks, O_SCS = 0.7 for r = λ/2 and O_SCS = 0.66 for r = λ at the design frequency.
DT tomograms show the approximate shape and size of the cloak, such as reduced radius and increased RI variation.
DT can detect cloaked objects even when SCS fails, especially at the design frequency.
For TO cloaks, DT is more sensitive than SCS for low losses, but SCS becomes more sensitive for high losses (o > -1.9).
The increased RI variation in DT tomograms makes closely packed cloaked objects more distinguishable.
The method could be extended to detect acoustic invisibility cloaks.
The design frequency for SC cloaks was f_0 = 783.8 THz (λ_0 = 382.7 nm).
The study used both Born and Rytov approximations for DT, with similar results.
Cloaking can enhance the contrast in tomographic images of closely packed particles.
The paper's findings could impact electronic warfare and biomedical imaging.
The relative observability O_DT is always greater than or equal to O_SCS for SC cloaks.
For polygonal TO cloaks, DT provides information on the shape of the device.
The study was conducted in 2D, but extension to 3D is straightforward.
The electric field was polarized along the z component for TE waves.
The detector line length was set to 10λ for SC cylinders, with a finite length w = 220λ used in simulations.
The RI profile of cloaked cylinders shows two lobes instead of one, indicating the presence of the cloak.
The paper's work was selected for the inside cover of Laser & Photonics Reviews.
The study suggests DT could lay the foundation for a unique design and characterization standard for invisibility cloaks.
The method could be used for particle counting or bioimaging due to enhanced contrast.
